candidates.author: Augustus, Emperor of Rome
candidates.coverage: Octavian's own brief account of the war, the oath of Italy and the western provinces, and the victory at Actium.
candidates.certainty: high; names Actium indirectly through the war against Cleopatra
candidates.reason: The Res Gestae is Octavian's own contemporary account of the war and the victory at Actium, a witness the graph does not yet read, and this copy is in English.

candidates.author: Velleius Paterculus
candidates.coverage: A pro-Augustan narrative of the battle, the desertions and Antony's flight, and the clemency shown afterwards.

candidates.reason: Velleius gives a near-contemporary prose narrative of the battle, the desertions and Antony's flight, which offsets the later Plutarch and Dio the graph already reads, and this copy is in English.

candidates.author: Horace
candidates.coverage: A poem written in the immediate aftermath of the battle, describing the defection of the Galatians and the enemy's flight.
candidates.reasonLeftOut: Horace's Epodes are a valuable contemporary poem, but this copy is Latin only, and Virgil already supplies the poetic voice.

candidates.author: Horace
candidates.coverage: The Cleopatra ode celebrating the victory and her flight and death.

copies.label: Gutenberg 5432: The Odes and Carmen Saeculare of Horace

candidates.reasonLeftOut: The Cleopatra ode is available in English, but the budget favours Virgil's fuller poetic treatment of the battle.

candidates.author: Propertius, Sextus
candidates.coverage: Elegies on Cleopatra's defeat and on Apollo's role at Actium (4.6).
candidates.reasonLeftOut: Propertius is another contemporary poet, available only in Latin, and his voice overlaps with Virgil's.

candidates.author: Josephus, Flavius
candidates.coverage: Herod's position during the Actian War and his meeting with Octavian afterwards.
candidates.certainty: medium; the battle is treated only peripherally
candidates.reasonLeftOut: Josephus covers Herod's side of the war rather than the battle itself, so he ranks below the direct witnesses.

candidates.author: Suetonius
candidates.coverage: The victory at Actium, the foundation of Nicopolis and the dedication of Octavian's campsite memorial.
identifiedAt: Scaife: Divus Augustus (urn:cts:latinLit:phi1348.abo012, work matched by title (verify))
candidates.reasonLeftOut: Suetonius is a later biographer whose material on Nicopolis and the campsite memorial largely overlaps with Strabo and the Res Gestae.

candidates.author: Florus, Lucius Annaeus
candidates.coverage: A rhetorical account of the fleets and the battle, drawn from Livy.
identifiedAt: Scaife: Epitome Rerum Romanorum (urn:cts:latinLit:phi1242.phi001, work found)
candidates.reasonLeftOut: Florus is a later Livian epitome available only in Latin, and the contemporary witnesses rank ahead of it.

candidates.author: Eutropius
candidates.coverage: A brief notice of Antony's defeat at Actium.

candidates.author: Orosius, Paulus

candidates.author: Shakespeare, William
candidates.coverage: A dramatization of the decision to fight at sea, Cleopatra's flight and Antony's shame.
candidates.reasonLeftOut: Shakespeare's play is an early modern dramatization rather than an ancient witness, so it ranks below the ancient sources within this budget.

notes: Ancient witnesses prioritized: Augustus's own Res Gestae and his lost memoir (cited in Plutarch Ant. 68), Velleius, the Augustan poets (Horace, Virgil, Propertius), Strabo, Suetonius and the Livian tradition (Periochae, Florus, Orosius). Weigall's citations point only to Plutarch, which is already read. Several cited-only-by-page modern works (Kebric, Potter, David & David, Fowler) were omitted as marginal.
